item.title: LB Cole Holcomb inactive for the Steelers on Friday
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The most notable absence on the Steelers side of the field on Friday afternoon will be Aaron Rodgers, but the team also has players still on their roster who will not be playing against the Broncos.
item.content:encoded:
The most notable absence on the Steelers side of the field on Friday afternoon will be Aaron Rodgers, but the team also has players still on their roster who will not be playing against the Broncos.

Linebacker Cole Holcomb was the only player on either team listed as questionable heading into the game and he will sit out with a heel injury. Holcomb has been a core special teamer for Pittsburgh this season.

With Rodgers gone, Will Howard moved up to the No. 2 quarterback spot. Drew Allar is inactive as the emergency third quarterback and wide receiver Kaden Wetjen, cornerback Sean Murphy-Bunting, running back Eli Heidenreich, linebacker Alex Highsmith, and defensive end Gabe Rubio are also out.

The Broncos' inactives are quarterback Sam Ehlinger, wide receiver Lil'Jordan Humphrey, safety Taylor Rapp, offensive lineman Gavin Ortega, offensive lineman Kage Casey, and tight end Dallen Bentley.

item.content:encoded:
The Browns will be on Sunday Night Football this weekend, but it remains to be seen if rookie wide receiver Denzel Boston will be in their lineup.

Boston missed his third straight practice on Friday with a quad injury and the team listed him as questionable to face the Raiders. The second-round pick has not missed a game this season and has 33 catches for 523 yards and three touchdowns in 10 contests.

Defensive end Derek Barnett (hamstring) also missed practice all week and has been ruled out for this Sunday.

Right guard Austin Barber (knee) and running back Raheim Sanders (hip) are listed as questionable. Sanders will need to be activated from injured reserve in order to play against Las Vegas.

item.title: Broncos, under Bo Nix, are much better at home than on the road
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Lost in the ongoing drama in Pittsburgh is that they play the 8-2 Broncos today.
item.content:encoded:
Lost in the ongoing drama in Pittsburgh is that they play the 8-2 Broncos today. Lost in that is that the Broncos, with Bo Nix at quarterback, are a much better team at home than they are on the road.

After playing 23 games in Denver, Nix has a 20-3 record with 43 touchdown passes and averaging 242.6 passing yards per game. Playing 23 games elsewhere, the Broncos are 13-10, with Nix throwing 27 touchdowns and averaging 195.9 passing yards per game.

The Steelers, in contrast, are 4-0 at home this year and 2-4 on the road.

With the forecast for the game similar to the conditions that played out in Buffalo on Thursday night, that could even things out, from a talent standpoint. And it could give the Steelers a chance to rebound from two days of total dysfunction with a season-altering win.

However it goes, the pressure is on Steelers coach Mike McCarthy. The best way to turn the page is to win. A loss (particularly an ugly one) will give even more credence to the things Aaron Rodgers said publicly on Wednesday.

item.content:encoded:
Patriots defensive tackle Christian Barmore was added to the team's injury report on Friday and his status for Sunday's game against the Chargers is uncertain as a result.

Head coach Mike Vrabel said that Barmore is dealing with a knee injury and he will be listed as questionable for this weekend. Barmore was not on the field during the open portion of Friday's practice.

Guard Alijah Vera-Tucker (hamstring) has not been activated from injured reserve, but Vrabel said that he will travel with the team to Los Angeles. Vera-Tucker will need to be activated by Saturday afternoon to play on Sunday.

Wide receiver Romeo Doubs (shoulder) has also been designated for return. Vrabel indicated he will not play and wide receiver A.J. Brown (hamstring), cornerback Carlton Davis (knee), and quarterback Drake Maye (fibula) have officially been ruled out.

item.title: Brian Schottenheimer on failed fourth-down try: "I trust our quarterback and our offense"
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The Eagles' path to erasing a 31-10 third-quarter deficit included many favorable twists and turns.
item.content:encoded:
The Eagles' path to erasing a 31-10 third-quarter deficit included many favorable twists and turns. The last one was a gift from the Cowboys.

With 55 seconds left — and with the Eagles having no timeouts — the Cowboys faced fourth and one from the Philadelphia 39. After attempting to get the Eagles to jump offside, the Cowboys took a timeout and decided to go for it.

The Cowboys lined up in shotgun formation. Quarterback Dak Prescott looked to the right, presumably to connect on a slant to receiver CeeDee Lamb. Lamb was jammed hard by cornerback Quinyon Mitchell. Prescott waited for Lamb to get free. When Prescott decided to pursue another option, he was sacked.

The play lost nine yards, giving the Eagles the ball at their own 48.

Why not punt? Why not force quarterback Joe Milton III to drive into field-goal range, with less than 50 seconds to play and no timeouts?

Coach Brian Schottenheimer was asked about the decision after the game.

"Really felt good about the drive we had going, and felt really good that we were gonna put the game away there," Schottenheimer told reporters. "And I wanted the ball in Dak's hands. And, unfortunately, we weren't able to make it work."

Does Schottenheimer ever second-guess himself?

"All the time," he said. "Not in that situation. Absolutely not in that situation."

Why not?

"I trust our quarterback and our offense," Schottenheimer said.

That's fine. But it's not about "trust." It's about whether it makes sense to assume the offense will execute in that moment, and what the consequence will be if the defense executes a little better.

It's about making an assessment, based on years of watching, playing, and coaching football, as to whether the risk of not converting outweighed the risk of the Eagles driving from their own 20 (or perhaps deep inside their own 20) into field goal range.

Maybe the truth is that Schottenheimer didn't trust his defense to keep that from happening. Regardless, his "trust" in the offense was ultimately misplaced. And the Cowboys lost another game when they scored 30 or more points.

item.title: Mike Tomlin on current Steelers situation: "It's a dumpster fire"
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Former Steelers coach speaks at length about this week's events.
item.content:encoded:
Many folks in and around football have had opinions about the recent brouhaha between former Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers and Steelers coach Mike McCarthy. Few have the insight and perspective that former Steelers coach Mike Tomlin brings to the table.

Appearing on NBC's Chiefs-Bills halftime show on Thanksgiving night, Tomlin shared his thoughts on the situation in a conversation with Mike Tirico. (A portion of it was on the live broadcast; the full interview is here.)

"I had a range of emotions watching those course of events yesterday," Tomlin told Tirico. "I think the prevailing one is just general sadness. Sad on a micro level, sad on a macro level. And by that, I mean, you know, just from an individual perspective, sad that we might be looking at the end of a legendary career of the quarterback, Aaron Rodgers, and just on the macro level, whether it's organizationally or for the game of football at large, to see laundry aired out that way in a public forum.

"Those are things that kind of run counterculture to professional football. So, just a lot of emotions, but probably more than anything, man, general sadness on a lot of levels."

Tirico asked Tomlin if he was shocked by Rodgers's decision to air dirty laundry in a public forum.

"It certainly did," Tomlin said, "but, you know, and particularly because I know both men involved, certainly had a lot of intimate work and development of relationship with Aaron over the last couple of years, and have known and competed against Mike, you know, respected and appreciated him as a coach for a long time. But I don't — what I acknowledge is I don't know them as a collective, the nature of their relationships, and so certainly I was surprised by that."

Regardless of Rodgers's conduct on the way out the door, Tomlin explained that Rodgers was viewed favorably by his teammates in 2025.

"He was beloved, and I'm not, you know, over-exaggerating that," Tomlin said. "He worked at it, and people appreciated his openness to getting to know and understand the Steeler culture, to be engaged with teammates, and particularly from my perspective, I worked with a lot of veteran players over the years and at times they lose a little patience for the process, or they lose patience for relationships with younger guys, et cetera. Man, he seemed to embrace all of that and really embrace it in a real, natural way. He was a tireless worker regarding the process.

"I called early-morning quarterback meetings on Wednesday and Thursday. He was always early and engaged. Did a heck of a job in terms of engaging and developing, assisting in the development of young players. Specifically, Will Howard was always in that meeting, and, shoot, man, [Rodgers] and I were shoulder-to-shoulder in terms of the development of Will and challenging Will to develop professional habits. And so, you know, it was early and extremely consistent during my time with him, in terms of his willingness to work in those areas, and I think that's why he's so beloved in that locker room, as been reported by multiple sources in light of this incident. That is real. The guys in that locker room love and appreciate Aaron Rodgers."

Had Tomlin gotten any sense that things were so close to breaking down?

"Absolutely none, but it's a really specific reason why, to be honest with you, man," Tomlin said. "One of my cultural mantras, when I worked there for the 19 years, is don't talk to people about your problems unless they can be a component of the solution. Because if you do, it's counterproductive, and people know where I stand there. And by that I mean if you have a problem with your playing time, don't talk to your teammate about it. Talk to somebody that can do something about it. That's problem solving.

"And so everybody understands my posture on some of that stuff, and so although I have really good, fluid communication with many of those guys, particularly, the more veteran guys, they know me and know me well enough to know that I didn't want to hear about any potential issues, because I'm not a component of the solution. And so although, particularly, like, Cam Heyward, he and I spent a little time together doing his bye week. Man, we had no mention of anything bubbling under the surface, if you will."

Can McCarthy effectively lead the team, given what Rodgers said?

"You know, it certainly created some challenges and challenges is probably an understatement if all of those things are true," Tomlin told Tirico. "And certainly the '1-2-3 Packers' is, because he acknowledged that. But his ability to overcome that or inability to overcome that in my opinion is based on relationships and the depth of those relationships and how those guys feel about him, or how those guys buy into what he's selling. And so, certainly, he's been there a short period of time. And so it makes you wonder, the level of that challenge. But it'll be relationship-based, his ability to overcome the things that you mentioned."

How does Tomlin think the Steelers will fare against the Broncos on Friday?

"Based on my knowledge of the men, particularly the leaders, the longstanding guys, they'll do a great job of getting hyper-focused on what really matters, and that's that football game," Tomlin said. "They'll use it as a mantra to bring them together. I expect those guys to fight. Now, fight and quality play are two different things. I'm certainly not gonna expect those guys not to fight. I think they're gonna fight and fight extremely hard. What I'm interested in is quality of play, quality of execution. And those are things that could be impacted by the level of distraction that they had on a short week in particular."

Tirico then asked Tomlin how he feels, overall, about what has transpired this week.

"I'm upset about it, you know, it's a dumpster fire," Tomlin said. "And I don't say that in a judgmental way. I presided over a few dumpster fires in my 19 years. But it certainly is upsetting, and I'm sure Steeler Nation is upset."

If owner Art Rooney II calls Tomlin for advice, what would Tomlin say?

"Hey, Mike, that's a hypothetical, because I know he wouldn't and, and because I know how he's trained," Tomlin said. "You know, Art is a guy that's not a hedge fund guy that bought a football team. He's not a, you know, artificial intelligence guy that bought a football team. This is a family business. It's generational. Any advice or thought process in that way, I imagine he just says, 'What would my dad do?' Or, 'What would my grandfather do?' Their mode of operation is time tested, it's generational. And so, I doubt, very, very seriously, that he called anyone for outside advice."

Finally, Tirico asked whether Tomlin believes Rodgers will get another NFL opportunity this season, if he wants one.

"There's certainly a possibility for that," Tomlin said. "And I just say that based on the 19 years that I held the position that I held. It's a 32-team league. All it takes is one. Over time, I've laughed and watched that people talk about, you know, 'No, that could never happen.' In a 32-team league, when everybody is highly competitive and there's some real challenges, particularly as you get to this portion of the journey from a player availability standpoint, there's certainly a possibility if he desires that he could play again, because all it takes is one suitor."

Having cleared waivers, Rodgers is available to that one suitor, if/when that one suitor calls. Still, that one suitor will need to be willing to accept the risk that, if Rodgers doesn't have things go the way he wants, he'll choose to do again the same thing he did this week.

item.title: T.J. Edwards: Fourth down pass to Jahmyr Gibbs a look we saw all week
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Bears had a hard time stopping Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs throughout Thursday's game in Detroit, so it made sense that the Lions put the ball in Gibbs's hands on fourth down with just over two minutes left to play.
item.content:encoded:
The Bears had a hard time stopping Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs throughout Thursday's game in Detroit, so it made sense that the Lions put the ball in Gibbs's hands on fourth down with just over two minutes left to play.

Gibbs caught a short pass with forward momentum and one player between him and a first down that would have pushed them much closer to a home win. That player was Bears linebacker T.J. Edwards and Edwards was able to corral Gibbs short of the sticks for a tackle that gave them a chance to steal a win with three seconds left on the clock.

After the 39-35 win, Edwards said he "knew it was going to be me" when he saw how the Lions lined up for the play.

“I knew that there’s gonna be a play that we would have to make,” Edwards said, via Kevin Fishbain of TheAthletic.com. “And we made a play when we needed to. I was happy to do it, grateful for it, man. It was a look that we saw all week, and I was able to make it.”

Gibbs picked up 252 yards on Thursday, but Edwards's recognition and execution meant the few he didn't get made all the difference.

item.title: Abdul Carter returns to Giants practice on Friday
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Giants welcomed linebacker Abdul Carter back to the practice field on Friday.
item.content:encoded:
The Giants welcomed linebacker Abdul Carter back to the practice field on Friday.

Carter was out of practice on Wednesday and Thursday due to illness and a calf injury, but reporters at the open portion of Friday's workout noted that he was working with the rest of the team. The Giants will release injury designations later in the day, but head coach John Harbaugh downplayed concern about Carter's availability earlier this week and Friday's change in status suggests he'll be ready to go against the Colts.

Carter had two sacks and five quarterback hits in last Sunday's win over the Jaguars. He was named the NFC defensive player of the week in recognition of that effort.

Reporters also noted that cornerback Dru Phillips was practicing after missing the last two days with an illness. Defensive tackle Shelby Harris has also been sick and was not spotted during the open portion of practice.

item.title: Art Rooney II expresses support for Mike McCarthy, calls Aaron Rodgers not a "good teammate"
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Steelers owner speaks about Wednesday's insanity.
item.content:encoded:
After Wednesday's unprecedented chaos, it had to happen. And it did.

Steelers owner Art Rooney II has addressed the events that resulted in the benching and then the firing of quarterback Aaron Rodgers.

“A change had to be made, and I certainly agree with the change and the way it was handled," Rooney told Gerry Dulac of the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette in a Thursday interview.

The change was sparked by the notion that Rodgers gave coach Mike McCarthy an ultimatum: “Either let me call all the plays or just release me.” Instead, McCarthy benched him.

It went to the next level when, as many expected, Rodgers scurried to the McAfee show to take shots at McCarthy for missing meetings, showing up late to meetings, and falling asleep in meetings — among other things, including the ultra-embarrassing "1-2-3 Packers!" moment from halftime of Sunday's loss to the Eagles.

“There’s maybe a time and place after the season if he wanted to kind of unload,” Rooney said. “He talks about wanting to be a good teammate, but you don’t do that to your teammates a couple days before the game, that’s for sure. . . .

“In general, I think, historically, what’s in the locker room stays in the locker room. That’s the way it’s always been. That’s the way it should be as far as I’m concerned.”

Rooney also confirmed that the team supports McCarthy, despite Rodgers's rant and reports confirming the facts underpinning the petty delivery of them.

“I just want to say that I have 100 [percent] confidence in Mike McCarthy and I expect he’ll be our coach this season, next season and beyond,” Rooney told Dulac. “The big thing, what happened this week, is insubordination can’t be tolerated in any organization. When you start getting ultimatums, you can’t live with that.”

Rooney also was asked whether Rodgers raised with the owner supposed concerns about McCarthy's health.

“Nothing,” Rooney said. “Mike’s as healthy as the rest of us. Health was not an issue. I’m not sure where that part comes [from].”

Rooney also addressed something that has been largely overlooked during the fast-moving drama: Rodgers's subpar performance.

“The sad thing is Mike took some of the bullets for Aaron in terms of some of the plays that were called, particularly in the red-zone troubles that we had,” Rooney said. “Mike took some of the bullets for things that were going wrong down there. He tried to protect him, and it just wasn’t working.”

They should have known it wouldn't work between Rodgers and McCarthy. It's still unclear why either one of them thought it would. McCarthy shouldn't have wanted a reunion with Rodgers. And Rodgers shouldn't have wanted a second act with McCarthy.

Then again, it's not as if Rodgers had many choices. In 2025, he had few takers. In 2026, he had fewer. If he was going to ensure that his final NFL throw wasn't a pick-six by playing another year, Pittsburgh wasn't just the best place.

It was likely the only place.

item.title: Jerry Jones on Mike McCarthy: "He was outstanding as the head coach"
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The recent remarks from former Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers regarding Steelers coach Mike McCarthy have raised plenty of questions, posed to plenty of people.
item.content:encoded:
The recent remarks from former Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers regarding Steelers coach Mike McCarthy have raised plenty of questions, posed to plenty of people.

After Thursday's 39-38 loss to the Eagles, Cowboys owner and G.M. Jerry Jones was asked about McCarthy, who coached Jones's team for five seasons, from 2020 through 2024.

"I offered him to stay at least another year when he left," Jones told reporters. "And so I thought he was outstanding as the head coach and had a great command of, frankly, quarterback, offense. Can't say enough good things about him. He's, frankly, one of the finest people that around football that I've been around. And I can't say enough about him. I never had the type of thing that is being said about him. I never had that in consideration in any of my time with him, extending his contract. Any of that, that was never on the table. And we never had an issue within the organization."

That conflicts, obviously, with the things Rodgers said on Wednesday.

Regardless, Jones no longer employs McCarthy. While Jones possibly chose to take the high road, a former employer vouching for a coach is fundamentally different than his current employer vouching for him.

McCarthy took the Cowboys to the playoffs three times in five years, advancing to the divisional round in 2022. The Cowboys failed to qualify for the postseason in the first year after McCarthy left. Thursday's loss to the Eagles makes it harder for them to get there the second post-McCarthy season.

item.title: Aaron Rodgers clears waivers
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Rodgers becomes a free agent.
item.content:encoded:
It's official. Aaron Rodgers is a free agent, again.

For the third time since March 2025, Rodgers can sign with any team at any time.

The soon-to-be 43-year-old cleared waivers on Thursday, per multiple reports.

He can sign whenever he chooses, either to a practice squad or a 53-man roster. He can wait until the postseason, if he chooses.

Of course, someone will have to want to sign him. In the 2026 offseason, only the Steelers did. At this point, an injury to a starter on a contending team will be the one thing that could create immediate interest in his services.

As long as that team is willing to risk Rodgers eventually dialing up McAfee for another elongated monologue of grievances. At this point, any other outcome would be a surprise.

item.title: Zach Ertz: People don't understand how good DeVonta Smith is
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Eagles wide receiver DeVonta Smith missed five games with a hamstring injury earlier this year and the Eagles lost all five of them, which doesn't feel like much of a coincidence after watching him in Dallas on Thursday.
item.content:encoded:
Eagles wide receiver DeVonta Smith missed five games with a hamstring injury earlier this year and the Eagles lost all five of them, which doesn't feel like much of a coincidence after watching him in Dallas on Thursday.

Smith caught 11 passes for 200 yards and two touchdowns in Philadelphia's remarkable 39-38 comeback win. The touchdowns came on 50- and 45-yard strikes from quarterback Joe Milton and Smith shook off a hard landing on his tailbone in the fourth quarter to finish out the game.

The 11 catches tied Smith's career best and the 200 yards were a personal record, but the big day didn't come as a shock to tight end Zach Ertz.

“It’s not surprising, honestly,” Ertz said, via Dave Zangaro of NBCSportsPhiladelphia.com. “I watched him when he was at Alabama, winning the Heisman. Comes in here right away, his game is just so smooth. I don’t think people understand how good of a player he truly is until he gets his opportunities. I don’t know what the final stats were. I know over 200 yards, which is crazy. But he’s just a receiver that really has no weakness. The way he runs routes is so smooth, the way he can make plays on the balls in the air, yards after catch. I think he’s probably one of the most underrated players in the league. I saw him as a rookie so where he’s at now doesn’t surprise me at all.”

The Eagles made Smith their No. 1 wideout when they traded A.J. Brown this offseason and the injury interrupted his bid to prove he's the right guy to fill that role on their offense, but Thanksgiving offered some proof of concept for the Eagles' passing game.

item.title: Bills benefited from extra seconds during Chiefs' final drive
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: For the second time this week, the clock operator took center stage.
item.content:encoded:
Every second counts.

We saw it on Monday night, when the clock operator didn't press the button to save a second or two for the Bengals to try to pull out a win over the Commanders.

It apparently happened again on Thursday night, in more subtle fashion.

By our count, the Buffalo clock operator managed to preserve four seconds during what was the Chiefs' final drive of the game.

I've watched it, several times. The Chiefs had first and 10 on their own 11. Quarterback Patrick Mahomes dropped the shotgun snap. By the time he recovered the ball, was touched, the whistle blew, and the Bills called a timeout (assuming they did it instantly), four seconds had elapsed. The clock, however, ultimately moved by only one second, from 26 to 25 — not 22.

Then, after running back Emmett Johnson gained five yards on second and 15, 19 seconds remained when the whistle blew. The clock in the NBC score bug at one point shifted from 19 seconds to 20, presumably to match the official time on the stadium scoreboard.

After the third-down incompletion, the clock showed 15 seconds. It should have been 11 seconds.

Following the punt, which was partially blocked, and the return by Greg Dortch, there were four seconds to play. Four seconds. The same four seconds that apparently were preserved through creative clock operation.

Of course, if the clock had shown 11 seconds and not 15 before the punt, the Bills may have not tried to block it. They may have opted to attempt a fair catch followed by a free kick.

Regardless, there was more time on the clock than there should have been. And those extra seconds ensured that the Bills would have just enough time for Tyler Bass to make a walk-off 57-yard field goal.

With so many games decided by such tight margins, there needs to be a better effort to ensure complete accuracy with the game timing, especially as the final seconds of a game tick, tick, tick away.

So when it was time to divvy up the postgame turkey legs, here's hoping the Bills saved a drumstick for the timekeeper.

item.title: The "carnival" came back to town on Thursday, and Joe Milton III won his "teddy bear"
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Cowboys' decision not to put Milton on the roster comes back to haunt them.
item.content:encoded:
Fifty-two years after the Thanksgiving legend of Clint Longley was born, a guy who couldn't convince the Cowboys to give him a spot on the 53-man roster pulled a Reverse Longley on America's Team.

On Thursday, former Cowboys practice-squad quarterback Joe Milton III returned to Dallas and made them regret not putting him on the roster when they had the chance.

The Cowboys acquired Milton in April 2025, sending a fifth-round pick to New England for Milton and a seventh-round pick. He appeared in four games last season before losing the training-camp and preseason competition with Sam Howell to be the backup to Dak Prescott.

Milton was released in late August. He cleared waivers. He joined the Dallas practice squad. After Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts landed on injured reserve due to blood clots, the Eagles came calling with a spot on the active roster. The Cowboys could have attempted to add Milton to their own active roster, but they didn't.

Milton's impressive performance has rekindled the comments made by Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer in the days before the 2026 rosters were cut from 90 to 53.

"I first remember hearing about Joe Milton he was at [the] University of Michigan, and everyone applauded him for how hard and how far he could throw the ball," Schottenheimer said at the time, via Jane Slater of NFL Network. "Cool. That's awesome. You know, go be in a carnival somewhere.  Like, that's not what playing NFL quarterback is. It's not, 'Yeah, I can throw the ball 85 yards.' You're throwing through small windows, you're throwing over people, you're changing arm slots.  So, like, to me, arm strength is cool but, like, you know, go to the fair and win a teddy bear."

In fairness to Schottenheimer, he then praised Milton's development.

"But you got to play quarterback, you know, and that's what I think you see Joe learning is he's playing quarterback," Schottenheimer said at the time. "And he's playing quarterback at a high level.  He's checking the ball down. He's making blitz adjustments. He's solving problems. He's reading, you know, from his first, second, to third and even fourth progression at times. And it takes time. I mean, it, you know, you don't stop. I mean, you don't stop learning as a quarterback and the only way to do it is to play and I'm really, really proud of him."

Still, the Cowboys weren't sufficiently proud of Milton to give him a roster spot. And owner/G.M. Jerry Jones refused to admit that they made a mistake.

"That is the best I've seen him play," Jones told reporters after the 39-38 loss. "And he picked a bad time to do it, from my standpoint."

From Milton's standpoint, he picked the ideal time to do it. He'll now become a factor in the Eagles' future plans at quarterback. How could he not be after what he accomplished on Thursday, engineering a comeback in a game that saw the Eagles down by 21 points late in the third quarter?

Still, it's just getting started for Milton. He needs to build on what he did. If he does, he'll become a long-time NFL starter. If he doesn't, he'll become another Clint Longley — whose Thanksgiving Day performance in 1974 wasn't the beginning but the end.

item.title: Patrick Mahomes on Harrison Butker: I try to have confidence in everybody, I know he's working at it
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: Harrison Butker missed yet another field goal on Thursday night, which was a key factor in the Chiefs eventually losing to the Bills, 13-10.
item.content:encoded:
Harrison Butker missed yet another field goal on Thursday night, which was a key factor in the Chiefs eventually losing to the Bills, 13-10.

With a whopping eight missed field goals in 11 games so far this season — plus one missed extra point — it’s fair to question how much longer the Chiefs can stick with their longtime kicker.

After the Thanksgiving loss, quarterback Patrick Mahomes offered some public support for the embattled kicker.

“I try to have confidence in everybody on the team. That’s part of playing this sport, is believing in the guys around you,” Mahomes said in his postgame press conference. “And obviously, Harrison hasn’t had the season that he’s wanted this year. But he’s also been one of the best kickers in the game for a long time.

“I know he’s working at it. I can tell you that. And he’s doing his best to be the best teammate he can be, and go out there and execute in those moments. Unfortunately, tonight it didn’t go his way. But, I promise you, he’ll come back and work at it again. And hopefully, the next time, he’ll be able to go out there and make it happen.”

The Chiefs signed Justin Tucker to their practice squad with the hope of pushing Butker to improve. But at this point, if Tucker is going to be around, it might be time to try him in a game.

item.title: Friday's game gives Steelers fans a chance to chime in on recent events
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Much has been said from the folks at the middle of the current clusterfudge at the confluence of three rivers.
item.content:encoded:
Much has been said from the folks at the middle of the current clusterfudge at the confluence of three rivers. One very important constituency has yet to chime in.

Later today, Steelers fans will get a chance to make their voices heard when the home team hosts the Broncos in a Black Friday game.

One option for Steelers fans will be to not show up. And we've heard some anecdotal evidence indicating that some fans have decided not to go to the game.

That may be better than the alternative. Steelers fans aren't blindly loyal. If they see something they don't like, they'll make it known. Loudly.

The dynamic adds extra pressure to the situation. If things start poorly, you'll hear the boos on the Prime Video stream, as clearly and plainly as we heard Rodgers’s comments during the Thursday night Prime Video game in Cleveland.

Last year, they booed during Renegade. Today, if the Steelers respond to the recent drama with a subpar showing, the booing will start a lot earlier than that strategic moment in the fourth quarter when they press "play" on their trademark rallying cry.

It's just another reason to tune in at 3:00 p.m. ET, and to watch — and listen — closely.

item.title: Dan Campbell on calling late timeouts: I was hoping for a "chance for rebuttal"
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: With 2:34 to play on Thursday, the Lions had the ball on the Chicago 39.
item.content:encoded:
With 2:34 to play on Thursday, the Lions had the ball on the Chicago 39. It was first and 10. Detroit led, 35-32.

In other words, Detroit had its ninth win in hand.

But the drive ended when coach Dan Campbell decided to go for it on fourth and four from the Chicago 33, instead of attempting a 51-yard field goal that would have stretched the lead to six.

Yes, the Bears would have gotten the ball back with more than two minutes to play, if Campbell had opted to kick (and if kicker Jake Bates had made it). Yes, a touchdown (and an extra point) would have won the game. By not converting, the Bears had a chance to play for overtime or, if they could gain enough ground, a game-winning touchdown.

After the game, Campbell addressed the decision to go for it on fourth down.

"I don't regret that, you know?" Campbell said. "I wish we would have made that. But, listen, sometimes that happens, you know?"

While that decision becomes the obvious focus of postgame scrutiny, a subsequent decision deserves some focus, too: As the Bears drove for what ultimately was the game-winning touchdown with three seconds left, Campbell called a pair of timeouts.

He called one after the Bears got a first down at the Detroit 31, with 1:12 to play. He called another after the Bears got a first down at the Detroit 21, with 52 seconds to play.

At the time, the Bears had only one timeout. Given the Thanksgiving Day debacle from 2024, when the Bears got greedy and blew their shot at a field goal that would have forced overtime (and coach Matt Eberflus got fired the next day), they undoubtedly wouldn't have gotten cute as the final minute ticked away.

Two years later, those two timeouts allowed the Bears to run the clock all the way down to the last few seconds before taking the lead.

Asked whether he took the timeouts to give the defense a "breather" or a chance to "regroup," Campbell said he was hoping for a "chance for rebuttal."

The problem with that approach is that it was premised on the Bears tying the game with a field goal. The timeouts helped ensure that the Bears would have enough time to score a touchdown.

There was still plenty of risk for Chicago. The Bears ran two plays with no timeouts, risking a sack or a tackle in the field of play that would have ended the game.

The first play flirted with disaster. With 13 seconds left and the Bears at the Lions' six, quarterback Caleb Williams threw toward running back D'Andre Swift near the goal line. The ball was tipped by linebacker Derrick Barnes. If it had gotten through to Swift, he may have caught it and been tackled short of the end zone. And the Bears most likely would have been unable to rush to the line, get in formation, snap the ball, and spike it.

Or the Swift catch could have been ruled a touchdown on the field and then overturned by replay review, with a 10-second runoff that would have ended the game. The Lions know that wrinkle all too well, thanks to an identical outcome in a 2017 game against the Falcons.

Still, the Bears scored a touchdown and won. And they had enough time to do it in part because Campbell called not one but two timeouts as the Bears were driving.

item.title: On Our Way Home is free on Thursday and Friday
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The holiday season is here.
item.content:encoded:
The holiday season is here. And I'm in the mood to give something away. (It must be the whiskey.)

The On Our Way Home ebook is available for free on Thursday and Friday.

Why not give something away? This is the week when everyone is trying to sell you something. No one is giving you anything, with zero strings attached.

On Our Way Home is primarily a Christmas story. It's also a ghost story. I cranked it out between Thanksgiving and New Year's Day a few years back.

In the interests of avoiding any spoilers, I'll just say this: Download it and give it a try. It's essentially about family and redemption and reconciliation. It's also about forgiving others, while finding a way to forgive yourself.

It's funny at times. It's sad at times. If you make it to the end, you'll possibly shed a tear or two.

The best feedback I've gotten came from a reader who had suffered from PTSD for years. Reading On Our Way Home unlocked his ability to feel emotions again.

I never intended anything like that. I just had an idea for a story, years before writing it. One year, I got caught up in the spirit of the season and it flowed, one chapter, one page, one word at a time.

The price is right. If you don't like it, delete it. If you like it, keep going.

Speaking of free, Quarterback of the Future is being posted, one chapter at a time. Twenty-five chapters are up. A new one is coming every day until it's done.

Someone asked recently why my break from writing consists of more writing. There's something magical and, frankly, fun about creating something out of nothing. It's even more fun when people read it and enjoy it.

Whether you enjoy it is up to you. If you don't, that's on me. But it won't cost you a penny to find out, if you download On Our Way Home on Thursday or Friday.

item.description: There is some nasty weather in Western New York on Thanksgiving night.
item.content:encoded:
There is some nasty weather in Western New York on Thanksgiving night.

Will one touchdown be enough to win it?

The Bills have at least scored one early in the second quarter, with James Cook going in for a 5-yard score.

It took Buffalo 11 plays to go 49 yards, with the team getting great field positions as a result of one play on special teams.

Chiefs returner Josh Downs let a punt fall and roll instead of fielding it in his team’s territory, which led the offense to start its second drive at the 4-yard line. Kansas City then went three-and-out, and the punt went out of bounds at the Kansas City 49.

The Bills only needed to convert one third down on their ensuing drive, with Josh Allen hitting Khaliil Shakir for a 17-yard pass on third-and-6.

While Buffalo got down to the 1-yard line, a false start backed them up. but Cook then erased that with his touchdown run.

In three drives, Cook has 42 yards on 13 carries with one touchdown. Allen is just 3-of-6 passing for 30 yards.

item.title: Bills lead Chiefs 7-3 at halftime on Thanksgiving night
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: Nasty weather in Western New York has limited offensive production for both Buffalo and Kansas City.
item.content:encoded:
There is some nasty weather in Western New York for Thanksgiving night and the Bills look like they have a home-field advance over the Chiefs.

Buffalo leads Kansas City 7-3 at halftime.

With steady freezing rain falling throughout the first half, it was difficult for both teams to get much going offensively. The game-time temperature was 35 degrees but the feels like temperature was down to 21.

The Bills have relied on running back James Cook for most of their offensive production. Cook rushed for 71 yards on 19 carries in the first half with a 5-yard touchdown.

Josh Allen is just 5-of-10 passing for 41 yards with an interception. Safety Alohi Gilman picked off Allen in the end zone on second-and-8 from the Kansas City 9 midway through the second quarter. At that point, it seemed like if the Bills scored a touchdown, they might have an insurmountable lead.

While the Chiefs didn’t score off of that interception, they at least kept Buffalo off the board.

But Kansas City had several miscues from the wet ball. The team had trouble fielding kicks, punter Matt Ariza had trouble catching a long snap before a punt, and Patrick Mahomes had trouble fielding a snap.

But Kansas City finally got a little something going late in the second quarter, with Harrison Butker sending a 26-yard field goal through the uprights to narrow Buffalo’s lead to four points.

Through 30 minutes, Mahomes is 10-of-15 for 97 yards. Travis Kelce has four receptions for 71 yards, including a key 21-yard catch at the end of the first half to get Kansas City into scoring position.

The Chiefs will receive the second-half kickoff.

item.title: Tyler Bass hits walk-off 57-yard field goal, Bills beat Chiefs 13-10
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: Buffalo overcame some nasty weather to once again defeat Kansas City in the regular season.
item.content:encoded:
The weather in Western New York delivered nasty conditions with freezing rain for Thanksgiving night.

It didn't matter to Tyler Bass.

Buffalo's kicker sent a walk-off, 57-yard field goal through the uprights to give the Bills a 13-10 victory over the Chiefs, putting the club further in the driver's seat for the AFC's No. 1 seed.

The game was not without controversy, particularly late in the contest. But the weather conditions also affected both teams, as neither offense got much going.

Josh Allen finished the game 10-of-21 for 81 yards with two interceptions, rushing for 43 yards on seven attempts. Allen’s passer rating of 18.3 is the second lowest of his career in any regular-season game.

Patrick Mahomes completed 16-of-29 passes for 174 yards with no touchdowns or interceptions.

James Cook ended up pacing the offense for Buffalo, rushing for 117 yards on 32 carries with Buffalo’s only touchdown — a 5-yard run in the second quarter.

The Chiefs got a 26-yard field goal from Harrison Butker to close the first half and a 1-yard touchdown from Emmett Johnson to open the second half. But the team was not able to score again.

After Bass connected on a 54-yard field goal in the fourth quarter to tie the game at 10-10, Butker missed his eighth field goal of the year — this one going wide right from 46 yards out.

Kansas City had the ball with another shot to get Butker in field goal range. But what looked like a third-down completion from Mahomes to Rahsee Rice was overturned on replay, allowing Buffalo to field another punt.

The Chiefs got yet another opportunity to possess the ball after Allen was sacked for the second time on the night. But the club’s special teams continued to have issues, with Josh Downs fielding a punt inside the 10, returning it to just the 11-yard line.

And when Mahomes’ third-down pass to an open Kelce fell incomplete, Matt Ariza’s punt was short and skipped to Greg Dortch, who returned 17 yards to the Kansas City 39 with four seconds on the clock.

Somehow in the weather conditions, that was enough for Bass, who sent the 57-yard attempt through the uprights to give the Bills their 10th win of the season.

Between Butker, Downs’ returns, and Ariza’s punts, the Chiefs special teams had a rough night, arguably costing the team the game.

On the injury front, Chiefs receiver/returner Jalen Royals (ankle) exited and was not able to return.

With the win, the Bills are now 10-1 and will have at least a one-game lead on the rest of the conference entering Week 13 for the No. 1 seed. Buffalo will play division-rival New England in Week 13.

The Chiefs are now 8-3 and won’t have extra rest in the coming week, as they’ll be in Los Angeles to face the Rams next Thursday night.

item.title: Kickers made the difference as Harrison Butker missed, Tyler Bass won the game
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: The Thanksgiving night game between the Bills and Chiefs was billed as the battle of two great quarterbacks, Josh Allen and Patrick Mahomes.
item.content:encoded:
The Thanksgiving night game between the Bills and Chiefs was billed as the battle of two great quarterbacks, Josh Allen and Patrick Mahomes. What proved to matter even more was the contrast of two kickers, as Buffalo's Tyler Bass was great and Kansas City's Harrison Butker was not.

On a rainy day in Buffalo, the fourth quarter featured Bass making a 54-yard field goal to tie the game 10-10, Butker missing a 46-yard field goal that would have given the lead back to the Chiefs, and then Bass making a 57-yard field goal as time expired to win the game, 13-10.

Bass has been excellent this season. He's now 26-for-27 on field goals in 2026, with his only miss coming from 54 yards in last week's win over the Dolphins.

Butker has been terrible this season. He's now 15-for-23 on field goals in 2026, and his eight misses are the most for any kicker in the league. He also hasn't made a single kick longer than 50 yards this season; 31 other NFL kickers have made at least one from beyond 50.

Chiefs coach Andy Reid said after the loss that he wasn't ready to say whether Butker will remain the kicker in Kansas City.

"I'll go back and go through all of it again," Reid said immediately after the game. "Not gonna make any decisions right this minute."

It's hard to see how the Chiefs can stick with Butker down the stretch. A kicker's job is to make his kicks, and Butker simply isn't performing.

item.title: Andy Reid: New York overturned Rashee Rice catch, not a call I agree with
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: The most pivotal call on Thanksgiving night was a replay review that went against the Chiefs.
item.content:encoded:
Chiefs coach Andy Reid was not happy with the NFL's officiating office in New York over a crucial call in the final minutes of the Thanksgiving night loss to the Bills.

With the Chiefs facing third-and-10 at their own 9-yard line with 1:51 remaining in the fourth quarter, Patrick Mahomes hit Rashee Rice over the middle for what the officials ruled was a sensational 11-yard catch. But the officiating office reviewed the play and ruled that Rice lost control as he was going to the ground. Reid said after the game that the on-field officials told him they thought it was a catch but the officiating office overruled them. Reid agreed with the officials on the field.

"Not one that I agreed with, but they said it came from New York," Reid said. "It's not from these guys, our guys called it a completion — the guys who were working the game. I'm not sure what they saw. I saw he had control of the ball, then his elbow hit, then the ball hit, but he had control. Normally, in those kind of situations, it's got to be clear and obvious. And to me, that was not clear and obvious.”

It was a big play, as it went from the Chiefs having first-and-10 at the 20-yard line with all three timeouts and a real chance of driving for a game-winning score on that possession, to the Chiefs having fourth-and-10 at their own 9-yard line and punting the ball back to the Bills. Ultimately, after an exchange of punts, it was the Bills who kicked the game-winning field goal as time expired. And it was Reid left to wonder what might have been if the call on the field had stood.
